sections.heading: Relational modeling: tables, keys, relationships
paragraphs: Relational databases store rows in tables. Each row gets a primary key — a unique, stable identifier. Relationships are expressed with foreign keys: an `orders.user_id` column pointing at `users.id` says every order belongs to a user.

Cardinality drives the shape: one-to-many is a foreign key on the 'many' side. Many-to-many needs a join table — `post_tags(post_id, tag_id)` — because neither side can hold a list of the other's keys in a single column cleanly.
Normalization means each fact lives in exactly one place. Storing the user's email on every order row means an email change must update thousands of rows — or, more realistically, quietly won't.
sections.summary: Link tables with keys, and when two things each have many of the other, connect them through a small `join table`.

variants.question: Posts can have many tags, and tags apply to many posts. What's the standard relational way to model this?
options: Duplicate each post row once for every tag it happens to carry
A tags column on posts holding a comma-separated string of tag names
A join table post_tags(post_id, tag_id) keyed to both tables
A posts column on each tag holding an array of the post ids
variants.rationale: Many-to-many decomposes into two one-to-many relationships through a join table. Each row of post_tags is one fact — 'this post has this tag' — indexable, constrainable, and queryable from both directions.
optionExplanations: Duplicating post rows destroys the primary key's meaning and multiplies every future update.
Comma-separated strings can't be foreign-keyed, can't be indexed usefully, and 'find posts tagged X' becomes string parsing in SQL — the classic anti-pattern.
Correct — the join table is *the* relational answer to many-to-many.
Arrays of ids can't enforce referential integrity, and querying 'tags for post 42' means scanning arrays in every tag row.
variants.interviewTip: Schema-design interviews almost always contain a hidden many-to-many. Say 'join table' early and draw it — it's often the main thing being tested.

variants.question: In a music app, a `song` can appear on many `playlist`s, and each `playlist` holds many `song`s. A junior dev proposes adding a `playlist_ids` integer column to the `songs` table. What's the correct relational model, and what's wrong with the proposal?
options: Add a `playlist_ids` column on `songs` and a `song_ids` column on `playlists` for both directions
Store the whole relationship as a JSON blob on `playlists`, which keeps the schema flexible
The proposal is fine as written, provided the `playlist_ids` column is indexed for lookups
Add a `playlist_songs(playlist_id, song_id)` join table; the scalar column can't be keyed
variants.rationale: A many-to-many between songs and playlists resolves into a join table whose every row is one membership fact. A single scalar column on `songs` can hold only one playlist id per row, and even packing many ids into it forfeits referential integrity and any efficient 'which songs are on playlist 7' lookup.
optionExplanations: Two mirror columns duplicate the same relationship in two unsynchronized places, doubling the update surface and inviting them to disagree.
A JSON blob can't be foreign-keyed, can't enforce that referenced songs exist, and turns 'playlists containing song X' into full-table JSON parsing.
Indexing a single integer column doesn't make it hold many values, and one song belongs to many playlists — the column can't represent the relationship at all.
Correct — the join table is the canonical resolution of many-to-many, queryable and constrainable from both sides.
variants.interviewTip: When two entities each own 'many' of the other, resist any single-column shortcut. Name the join table and note it can carry its own columns (e.g. `position`, `added_at`) — that extra insight signals depth.

variants.question: An e-commerce schema must place `products` under `categories`: a product can sit in several categories, and each category contains many products. Which design captures this correctly — and what does it unlock beyond mere linkage?
options: A `product_categories(product_id, category_id)` join table that can carry a `featured` column
A single `category_id` foreign key on `products`, since every product has one primary category
A `category_names` text array column on `products`, GIN-indexed for fast containment lookups
A `product_ids_csv` column on `categories`, refreshed each night by a scheduled batch job
variants.rationale: Many-to-many resolves into a join table where every row is one membership fact, enforceable and queryable from both directions. The join table is also the natural home for attributes of the relationship itself — `featured`, `sort_order` — which belong to neither product nor category alone.
optionExplanations: Correct — the join table models the many-to-many cleanly, and relationship attributes live on it, not on either entity.
A single foreign key models one-to-many only; the moment a product needs a second category, the design collapses or spawns duplicate product rows.
An array of names sidesteps foreign keys entirely: renaming a category strands stale strings, and nothing stops a row from referencing a category that no longer exists.
A CSV column maintained by a batch job is relationally unqueryable, up to a day stale, and enforces no integrity at any point in its lifecycle.
variants.interviewTip: Level up the join-table answer by asking where relationship attributes go: 'is this product *featured* in this category?' can only live on the join table. Volunteering that question shows you model facts, not just links.

variants.question: A university system tracks which `students` enroll in which `courses`. A proposal argues that since Postgres supports arrays, an `enrolled_course_ids integer[]` column on `students` is simpler than another table. Which statement identifies the decisive flaw?
options: Arrays are fine here because Postgres can index them, making the design equivalent to a join table
Array elements can't join in foreign-key constraints, so those course ids are never guaranteed to exist
The flaw is purely one of performance — arrays are slower to scan, but data integrity is fully unaffected
The array simply belongs on the other side: store `student_ids` on `courses`, which reads more naturally
variants.rationale: No relational engine enforces foreign keys on array elements: drop a course and every student row silently keeps a dangling id, with no error and no cascade. The join table is the only design the database itself can police, and it answers 'who takes course 12?' as cheaply as 'what does student 7 take?'.
optionExplanations: GIN indexes make containment lookups possible, but indexing does not create referential integrity — the two designs are not equivalent.
Correct — foreign-key enforcement and cascades only exist for scalar columns; the join table is the design the engine can actually guarantee.
The deeper defect is integrity, not speed: deleted courses leave dangling ids behind with no error raised, silently corrupting enrollment data.
Mirroring the array onto the other table inherits every flaw and adds a second unsynchronized copy of the same relationship.
variants.interviewTip: If an interviewer floats the tempting array-column shortcut, name the two things it forfeits — foreign-key enforcement and symmetric querying — then draw `enrollments`. Explaining *why* the shortcut fails scores higher than merely rejecting it.

sections.heading: Joins: recombining what normalization split
paragraphs: Normalization splits facts into separate tables; joins put them back together at query time. `INNER JOIN` returns only rows with a match on both sides. `LEFT JOIN` returns every row from the left table, with NULLs where the right side has no match.

The choice changes the question being asked. Users INNER JOIN orders: 'users who have ordered'. Users LEFT JOIN orders: 'all users, with their orders if any' — which is what a report like 'order count per user, including zero' needs.
Aggregation composes on top: `GROUP BY` collapses row groups, `COUNT`/`SUM` summarize them, and `HAVING` filters the groups after aggregation (where `WHERE` filters rows before it).
sections.summary: Use `LEFT JOIN` when you want to keep every row from one table even if the other side has no match.

variants.question: A 'signups vs activity' report must list ALL users with their order counts — including users with zero orders. Which query shape is right?
options: users LEFT JOIN orders, GROUP BY users.id, COUNT(orders.id)
Two separate queries — one per branch — stitched with UNION
orders LEFT JOIN users, GROUP BY orders.id, COUNT(users.id)
users INNER JOIN orders, GROUP BY users.id, COUNT(orders.id)
variants.rationale: LEFT JOIN preserves every user; those without orders get NULL order columns, and COUNT(orders.id) counts non-NULL values — yielding 0 for them. INNER JOIN would silently drop exactly the zero-order users the report exists to find.
optionExplanations: Correct — and the detail matters: COUNT(orders.id), not COUNT(*), which would count the NULL row as 1.
A UNION of 'users with orders' and 'users without' can be forced to work but is a contorted rewrite of what LEFT JOIN says directly.
This direction preserves all *orders* (which all have users anyway) and groups by the wrong entity.
INNER JOIN excludes users with no matching order — the report's most interesting rows vanish, and nothing errors to warn you.
variants.interviewTip: 'When would you use a LEFT JOIN over an INNER JOIN?' — give the concrete report: 'all users including those with zero orders.' The COUNT(column) vs COUNT(*) NULL subtlety is a bonus point interviewers notice.

variants.question: A dashboard needs the number of published comments for every blog `article`, and articles with no comments yet must show `0`. A teammate writes `articles LEFT JOIN comments ... GROUP BY articles.id` but uses `COUNT(*)`, and complaints come in that commentless articles show `1`. What actually went wrong?
options: `LEFT JOIN` was the wrong choice here; an `INNER JOIN` would have shown the correct zero counts
`COUNT(*)` counts the NULL row `LEFT JOIN` makes as `1`; `COUNT(comments.id)` yields `0`
`GROUP BY articles.id` is invalid on a joined table and silently returns exactly 1 per group
The counts are off because `HAVING`, not `GROUP BY`, was the clause needed to collapse the rows
variants.rationale: For an article with no comments, `LEFT JOIN` still emits one row with every `comments` column NULL. `COUNT(*)` counts rows regardless of NULLs, so it counts that placeholder as 1. `COUNT(comments.id)` counts only non-NULL values of that column, correctly returning 0.
optionExplanations: `INNER JOIN` would drop the commentless articles entirely — the dashboard would show them as missing, not as 0, which is a worse failure.
Correct — the join shape was right; the bug is `COUNT(*)` versus `COUNT(comments.id)` over the NULL placeholder row.
Grouping by the primary key of the left table is valid and standard; it isn't the cause and doesn't force a count of 1.
`HAVING` filters groups after aggregation; it wouldn't fix an inflated per-group count, and none was needed here.
variants.interviewTip: The `COUNT(*)` vs `COUNT(column)` trap is a favorite because both 'look right'. Say it out loud: over a `LEFT JOIN`, count the joined table's key column, never `*`.

variants.question: A staffing report must show every support `agent` with the number of `tickets` they resolved this month — managers specifically want to spot agents with zero resolutions. The query uses `agents INNER JOIN tickets ... GROUP BY agents.id` and passes code review as 'looking correct'. What will production reveal?
options: Nothing — INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN produce identical results once the GROUP BY is applied
The query errors at runtime, because aggregating over an INNER JOIN requires a HAVING clause
Zero-resolution agents appear with a NULL count instead of 0, which merely confuses the formatting
Zero-resolution agents are absent entirely — no row, no zero; use `agents LEFT JOIN tickets`
variants.rationale: INNER JOIN emits only agents with at least one matching ticket, so precisely the rows the report exists to surface are missing — and nothing fails loudly. LEFT JOIN preserves every agent; matchless agents get a NULL-filled row, and `COUNT(tickets.id)` turns that into the desired 0.
optionExplanations: GROUP BY collapses whatever rows the join produced; it cannot resurrect agents the INNER JOIN never emitted in the first place.
Aggregating over an INNER JOIN without HAVING is perfectly legal; the query runs cleanly, which is exactly what makes the bug dangerous.
A NULL row would at least leave a visible trace; INNER JOIN removes the agent's row entirely, so there is nothing on screen to notice.
Correct — the failure is silent row loss, and only the LEFT JOIN plus COUNT(column) shape restores agents with zero tickets.
variants.interviewTip: Frame INNER JOIN's failure mode as *silent row loss*: no error, no NULL, just missing entities. Interviewers reward candidates who identify that the most interesting rows of a report are often the ones a join can quietly delete.

variants.question: To list all `warehouses` with their count of delayed `shipments` (zeros included), someone writes: `warehouses LEFT JOIN shipments ON shipments.warehouse_id = warehouses.id WHERE shipments.status = 'delayed' GROUP BY warehouses.id`. Warehouses with no shipments vanish from the output anyway. Why?
options: COUNT was applied before the GROUP BY step, and that ordering quietly discards the empty groups
LEFT JOIN only preserves left rows when the right table is empty overall, never on a per-row basis
The `WHERE` on `shipments.status` drops the NULL rows (`NULL = 'delayed'` is untrue); use `ON`
`GROUP BY warehouses.id` must instead read `GROUP BY shipments.warehouse_id` for the outer join to hold
variants.rationale: For a matchless warehouse, LEFT JOIN emits one row with every `shipments` column NULL. The WHERE clause then evaluates `NULL = 'delayed'`, which is not true, and discards that row — outer-join semantics destroyed after the fact. Moving the predicate into `ON` filters shipments *before* the join, so every warehouse survives with its (possibly zero) delayed count.
optionExplanations: Aggregation order isn't the issue — the placeholder rows were removed by the WHERE clause before COUNT ever saw them.
LEFT JOIN preserves every left row per-row by design; the preservation was undone downstream, not skipped by the join.
Correct — a WHERE predicate on the right table's columns silently reimposes inner-join behavior; filter the right side in the ON clause instead.
Grouping by the left table's primary key is the standard, correct shape; changing the grouping column would not bring the lost rows back.
variants.interviewTip: 'What's the difference between filtering in ON versus WHERE for an outer join?' is the question behind the question. Answer: ON filters before the join (rows still preserved), WHERE filters after (NULL rows die) — knowing this cold is a strong signal.

sections.heading: Indexes: the speed/write tradeoff
paragraphs: Without an index, `WHERE email = ?` scans every row. An index is a sorted structure (typically a B-tree) on chosen columns that lets the database seek directly — the difference between reading a phone book and reading every page of it.

Indexes aren't free: every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must also maintain each index, and they consume storage. You index the columns your queries actually filter, join, and sort on — driven by evidence like `EXPLAIN` output and slow-query logs, not by decoration.

Composite indexes follow the leftmost-prefix rule: an index on `(user_id, created_at)` accelerates filters on `user_id` and on `user_id + created_at`, but does nothing for a filter on `created_at` alone.
sections.summary: Indexes make reads fast but slow writes a little, so add them for the columns you actually search on.

variants.question: A query filtering `WHERE user_id = ? AND created_at > ?` is slow. The table has an index on (created_at, user_id). The DBA suggests (user_id, created_at) instead. Why would column order matter?
options: The index (created_at, user_id) is invalid SQL, so it was never actually being used at all
It doesn't matter here — column order within a composite index is purely cosmetic and inert
With user_id first, the index groups a user's rows so the created_at range scans one slice
Composite indexes can only ever use their single first column, and never any that follow it
variants.rationale: A B-tree sorts by the first column, then the second within it. Leading with the equality filter (user_id) narrows to one contiguous slice, and the range on created_at scans just that slice. Leading with the range column scatters the target user's rows across the whole date range.
optionExplanations: It's valid and may even get partially used — just poorly for this query shape.
Order is one of the most consequential choices in index design — the leftmost-prefix rule depends on it entirely.
Correct — the rule of thumb: equality columns first, then the range column.
Composite indexes serve multi-column lookups all the time; the constraint is the leftmost prefix, not first-column-only.
variants.interviewTip: 'How would you speed up this slow query?' — the professional answer starts with 'first I'd run EXPLAIN', then discusses index shape. Leading with evidence beats leading with a guess.

variants.question: A table has a composite index on `(tenant_id, status, created_at)`. Three queries run against it: (A) `WHERE tenant_id = ?`, (B) `WHERE status = ? AND created_at > ?`, (C) `WHERE tenant_id = ? AND status = ?`. Which query can the index NOT accelerate, and why?
options: Query C, because an index needs all three of its columns present in the filter to be used
All three are accelerated equally well; the column order within the index is entirely irrelevant
Query A, because a single-column filter can never make use of a three-column composite index
Query B, because it skips the leading `tenant_id`, and leftmost-prefix bars seeking without it
variants.rationale: A B-tree composite index is sorted by its leading column first. Query B filters on `status` and `created_at` but never constrains `tenant_id`, so it can't use the sorted structure to seek — the leftmost prefix is missing. A uses the prefix `(tenant_id)`, and C uses the prefix `(tenant_id, status)`, so both are served.
optionExplanations: An index does not require every column to be present; any contiguous prefix from the left suffices, so C's two-column prefix works.
Column order is decisive here — it's the entire reason B fails while A and C succeed.
Query A filters exactly the leading column, which is the shortest valid leftmost prefix — the index accelerates it well.
Correct — B omits the leading `tenant_id`, breaking the leftmost-prefix requirement, so the index can't be seeked for it.
variants.interviewTip: Reframe leftmost-prefix as 'you may drop columns from the right, never from the left.' Being able to classify several queries against one index quickly is exactly the drill interviewers run.

variants.question: A `signups` table carries a composite index on `(country, signup_date)`. The nightly analytics job runs `WHERE signup_date >= ? AND signup_date < ?` with no country filter, and `EXPLAIN` shows a full table scan. What explains this, and what's the honest fix?
options: Range operators disable B-tree indexes; rewriting the range as one equality check per day fixes it
The index leads with `country`, so a date-only query has no leftmost prefix; put `signup_date` first
The index has become corrupted over time; running a REINDEX will restore its use for this query shape
Composite indexes only ever apply to JOIN queries, and never to a plain single-table WHERE filter
variants.rationale: A B-tree on `(country, signup_date)` is sorted by country first; within it, dates repeat per country. A date-only filter has no leading value to seek to, so its target rows are scattered through the entire structure — the planner rightly prefers a scan. Serving this query well means an index whose leftmost column is `signup_date`.
optionExplanations: Range predicates are a core strength of sorted B-tree indexes and use them constantly; the operators are not the problem here.
Correct — without the leading `country`, there is no contiguous region to seek; the leftmost-prefix rule makes the existing index useless for this shape.
Nothing suggests corruption — the plan reflects index shape, and REINDEX would rebuild the same shape that cannot serve this query.
Composite indexes accelerate plain WHERE filters routinely; a join-only restriction does not exist.
variants.interviewTip: When EXPLAIN shows a scan on a table that 'has an index', check the index's leading column against the query's filters before anything else — a mismatch there explains most 'but we indexed it!' mysteries.

variants.question: You may add exactly ONE index to speed `WHERE status = 'open' AND assignee_id = ? AND due_at < ?` on a large `tasks` table — two equality filters and one range. Which column order serves the query best?
options: `(assignee_id, status, due_at)` — both equality columns first, the range column last, for one narrow slice
`(due_at, assignee_id, status)` — the range column should lead, since ranges are the most selective filters
`(due_at)` alone — a single-column index always outperforms a composite one on a large table like this
Any order works fine; the optimizer internally reorders a composite index's columns to match each query
variants.rationale: Equality columns pin exact values, narrowing to one contiguous run of the B-tree; the trailing range column is then a short in-order scan within that run. Lead with `due_at` and you get a wide band of dates in which the target assignee's open tasks are scattered — the equality filters can no longer seek.
optionExplanations: Correct — equality-before-range puts all matching rows in one sorted slice, with the range as a cheap final walk.
Leading with the range yields a broad band of dates where the wanted assignee and status are interleaved with everyone else's rows — most of the band is wasted reads.
A lone `due_at` index selects a wide date window and then forces row-by-row filtering on assignee and status for everything in it.
The optimizer chooses among existing indexes; it cannot re-sort a B-tree's column order at query time — order is fixed at creation.
variants.interviewTip: Compress the rule to five words — 'equality first, range column last' — then justify it with the B-tree picture: exact matches nail down a contiguous region, the range walks it. The picture is what convinces the interviewer you're not reciting.

sections.heading: Transactions: all or nothing
paragraphs: A transaction groups statements into an atomic unit: BEGIN, statements, COMMIT — or ROLLBACK, which undoes all of them. The textbook case is a money transfer: debit one account, credit another. A crash between the two without a transaction silently destroys money.

ACID names the guarantees: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (constraints hold), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-done work), Durability (committed means persisted).

In Prisma this is `prisma.$transaction([...])` or the interactive `prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => {...})`; in Drizzle, `db.transaction(async (tx) => {...})`. Same contract: throw inside, and everything rolls back.
sections.summary: Wrap related writes in a transaction so they all succeed together or all undo, never leaving things half-finished.

variants.question: An order checkout does three writes: create order, decrement inventory, record payment. The server can crash at any moment. What guarantees the database never ends up with an order whose inventory was never decremented?
options: Wrap all three writes in one transaction, so a crash before COMMIT rolls them all back
Add a try/catch around the writes and log any errors for a human to clean up manually
Use three separate databases so that a failure in one stays isolated from the others
Run the three writes in quick succession to keep the window of risk as small as it can be
variants.rationale: Atomicity is precisely this guarantee: until COMMIT, none of the writes are permanent; a crash mid-way leaves the database as if nothing happened. Shrinking timing windows or logging for cleanup are mitigations — a transaction is the actual solution.
optionExplanations: Correct — atomic commit/rollback is what transactions are for.
try/catch can't catch a process crash or power loss, and 'manual cleanup' means a human reconciling corrupted money data.
Splitting across databases makes atomicity *harder* (now you need distributed transactions) — the opposite of a fix.
A smaller window is still a window; under real traffic, 'rare' inconsistency becomes 'weekly' inconsistency.
variants.interviewTip: When 'transaction' comes up, name-drop the boundary decision too: keep transactions short and never hold one open across an external API call — that's where senior candidates differentiate.

variants.question: A signup flow inserts a `user` row, then inserts a matching `wallet` row seeded with a starting balance. In production, some users exist with no wallet at all. The code already wraps both inserts in `db.transaction(async (tx) => {...})`. Which ACID property is being violated, and what's the most likely cause?
options: Durability is failing here; the committed wallet rows are being quietly lost after the fact
Atomicity is defeated: the wallet insert runs on the outer `db`, not `tx`, so it's outside the unit
Isolation is the problem here; a second concurrent transaction is deleting the wallet rows as they land
Consistency is fine, and users existing without a wallet is simply expected transaction behavior
variants.rationale: Atomicity means all statements in the transaction commit or none do. If the wallet insert accidentally uses the outer `db` handle rather than the transaction's `tx` handle, it executes outside the atomic unit — so it can fail (or its enclosing scope can throw after it) while the user insert still commits, producing users without wallets.
optionExplanations: Durability concerns committed data surviving crashes; here the wallet was never committed as part of the unit, so nothing durable was lost.
Correct — using `db` instead of `tx` for the inner write silently excludes it from the atomic unit, breaking all-or-nothing.
Isolation governs visibility of concurrent in-flight work; nothing here indicates a competing transaction deleting rows.
A partial result — user without wallet — is exactly what a correctly-scoped transaction is supposed to prevent, so this is not expected.
variants.interviewTip: The subtle real-world transaction bug isn't forgetting to open one — it's writing through the wrong handle inside it. Always thread `tx` (not the outer client) into every call in the block.

variants.question: A loyalty-points transfer runs inside `db.transaction(async (tx) => {...})`: debit the sender via `tx`, then credit the receiver via `tx`. The credit occasionally fails, yet production shows senders debited with no matching credit. The credit call is wrapped in its own `try/catch` that logs the error and continues. What's actually happening?
options: Durability is broken — the credit did commit, but was lost when the server later restarted
The database auto-commits every statement, so a transaction cannot span multiple awaited calls
The inner `catch` swallows the failure, so the callback returns and COMMITs the debit alone
The two writes need separate transactions, so the credit's failure can't affect the debit at all
variants.rationale: Interactive transaction APIs roll back when the callback throws. Catch the failure inside and suppress it, and the driver sees a callback that completed successfully — so it commits whatever did succeed. Atomicity wasn't defeated by the database; it was defeated by error handling that stopped the signal from reaching the transaction boundary.
optionExplanations: Durability failures lose committed data across crashes; here the credit statement failed before any commit, and the debit was committed deliberately by a 'successful' callback.
Transactions span awaits on the same `tx` handle just fine — supporting exactly that is why interactive transaction APIs exist.
Correct — rollback is triggered by an escaping exception; a swallowing catch converts a failed unit of work into a partial commit.
Separate transactions would *guarantee* the partial outcome you're trying to prevent — the debit and credit must live or die together.
variants.interviewTip: Inside a transaction callback, catch-and-continue is a rollback killer. If you must catch (to log or wrap), rethrow — the exception escaping the callback IS the rollback mechanism.

variants.question: A flash sale has `stock = 1` for an item. Two checkouts run concurrently: each SELECTs the stock (both read 1), each decides it can sell, each runs `UPDATE stock = stock - 1` and inserts an order — both COMMIT, and stock lands at `-1`. Every statement ran inside a transaction. Which ACID property is at issue, and why didn't 'using transactions' save you?
options: Atomicity — one of the two transactions must have partially committed only some of its statements
Durability — the first decrement wasn't flushed to disk before the second transaction read the stock
Consistency — the database defines an implicit non-negative rule on numeric columns that this bypassed
Isolation — default levels permit this read-then-write race; guard with `UPDATE ... WHERE stock > 0`
variants.rationale: Both transactions were atomic and durable — each committed everything it did. The anomaly lives *between* them: under common default isolation (read committed), both may read the same stale stock and proceed, a classic lost-update race. Transactions bound a unit of work; they do not automatically serialize concurrent decision logic built on plain reads.
optionExplanations: Both transactions committed all of their statements in full; nothing was partial — which is exactly why the outcome looks legal to the database.
Durability concerns committed data surviving crashes; both commits persisted precisely as written.
Databases enforce only the constraints you declare, and none was declared here — transactions never 'bypass' constraints in any case.
Correct — this is a concurrency anomaly under weak isolation; the check-and-decrement must be a single atomic operation the database arbitrates, not a hopeful read followed by a write.
variants.interviewTip: 'We used transactions — how did we oversell?' is a postmortem staple. The senior answer separates the A from the I: transactions made each checkout all-or-nothing, but only locking, guarded updates, or stricter isolation orders them against each other.

sections.heading: ORMs, migrations, and the N+1 trap
paragraphs: ORMs like Prisma and Drizzle map tables to typed objects: `prisma.user.findMany({ where: ... })` instead of hand-built SQL strings. You gain type safety, autocompletion, and injection-safe parameterization; you give up some control over the exact SQL emitted.

Migrations version your schema the way git versions code: each change (add column, create table) is a replayable script, so dev, staging, and prod evolve identically. Editing production schemas by hand is how environments drift apart irreversibly.

The signature ORM performance bug is N+1: fetch 100 posts (1 query), then lazily fetch each post's author inside a loop (100 more). ORMs make the loop invisible — the fix is telling the ORM up front to include the relation (`include`/`with`), collapsing it into a join or two queries.
sections.summary: When loading a list plus related data, ask for the related data up front (`include`/`with`) so you avoid hundreds of extra queries.

variants.question: A page lists 100 posts with author names. Logs show 101 queries per page load. What's happening, and what's the fix?
options: The ORM's query cache is disabled; enabling it will remove the repeated author queries
The connection pool is misconfigured for this load; raising the pool size clears the backlog
Classic N+1: one query for posts, then one per author. Fix: eager-load with include/with
The database is missing an index on posts.id, so each lookup scans the whole posts table
variants.rationale: 1 + 100 = the N+1 signature. Each author lookup happens lazily inside the render loop. Eager loading declares the relation need up front, letting the ORM emit a join (or one batched IN query) instead of a hundred round-trips.
optionExplanations: Caching may mask it for repeated authors, but the first cold load still storms the database — and correctness now depends on cache state.
A bigger pool lets the 101 queries run more concurrently — you've optimized the symptom's throughput, not removed the 100 extra queries.
Correct — recognize the 1+N count, name the pattern, eager-load the relation.
Each per-author query is likely already an indexed fast lookup; the cost is 100 round-trips, not 100 slow queries.
variants.interviewTip: N+1 is arguably the single most-tested ORM concept in interviews. Be able to define it in one sentence and give the fix in the next.

variants.question: An API serializes 50 `order`s, and for each order accesses `order.customer.tier` and `order.shippingAddress.country`. Query logs show 101 queries per request. A developer adds `include: { customer: true }` and the count drops to 51, not 1. What's the remaining issue and the complete fix?
options: The remaining 50 queries come from a missing index on the `orders.id` primary-key column
Dropping to 51 proves the ORM cache is now working; clearing that cache would restore 101
51 is already the optimal count; adding a second `include` here would only make it run slower
Only `customer` was eager-loaded, so `shippingAddress` stays lazy — add it to the include
variants.rationale: The original 101 was 1 + 50 (customer) + 50 (address). Eager-loading only `customer` collapses one of the two N-loops, leaving 1 + 50 = 51 from the still-lazy `shippingAddress` access. Including every accessed relation in the same query removes the remaining per-row round-trips.
optionExplanations: The per-order lookups are keyed, indexed point reads; the cost is 50 extra round-trips, not a missing index.
The drop came from eager-loading `customer`, not caching; there's no cache toggle at play here.
51 still carries a full N+1 for the address relation; it is not optimal, and adding the second `include` reduces round-trips, not increases them.
Correct — a partial eager-load fixes only the relations named; every relation touched in the loop must be included.
variants.interviewTip: Partial fixes to N+1 are a classic trap: eager-loading one relation while another stays lazy. Enumerate every relation the serializer touches and include them all in a single fetch.

variants.question: A hotfix needs a `refunded_at` column on `payments`. A teammate connects directly to the production database, runs `ALTER TABLE payments ADD COLUMN refunded_at timestamptz`, and ships the code. Weeks later, staging deploys start failing and a new developer's local setup breaks on the same missing column. What was the mistake, and what's the disciplined alternative?
options: Nothing was wrong — altering production first, then backfilling other environments later, is standard practice
The change bypassed migrations, so no versioned script exists to replay; commit one and run it everywhere
The column type was the real mistake; `timestamptz` can't be added to an existing table without downtime
Migrations only matter for destructive changes; an additive column is safe to apply by hand in any environment
variants.rationale: Migrations version the schema the way git versions code: every environment converges by replaying the same ordered scripts. A hand-run ALTER exists only in production's memory — staging, CI, and fresh local databases have no record of it, so they drift until something visibly breaks, usually far from the original change.
optionExplanations: That order guarantees drift: the artifacts that define the schema (committed migrations) were never told the change happened.
Correct — schema changes must live as replayable, committed scripts so dev, staging, and prod evolve through identical history.
Adding a nullable column is typically an instant metadata-only change; the type wasn't the problem — the missing migration was.
Additive changes drift just as thoroughly as destructive ones: other environments now lack a column the code expects, which is precisely the observed breakage.
variants.interviewTip: Own the phrase 'environments converge by replaying the same history.' If asked about hotfixes, concede the emergency ALTER can happen — but the follow-up migration that codifies it must land in the same PR, or the drift clock starts ticking.

variants.question: An admin table renders `n` invoices with each customer's name. Metrics show query count tracking page size exactly: 26 queries when `n = 25`, 101 when `n = 100`. A teammate proposes doubling the connection pool and putting Redis in front of the customer lookups. What's the sharper diagnosis and fix?
options: Query count scaling as `1 + n` is the N+1 fingerprint; declare the relation up front via include/with
Pool exhaustion is the root cause; doubling the connections will bring the per-page query count down
Redis is the right call here — caching customer names eliminates the pattern rather than masking it
The per-invoice queries indicate a missing index on `customers.id` that the table's primary key fails to cover
variants.rationale: The tell isn't any single number — it's the scaling law: one list query plus exactly one query per row rendered. That's a lazy relation access inside the loop. Pools and caches change how the extra queries are absorbed; eager loading is the only proposal that removes them.
optionExplanations: Correct — linear growth of queries with rows rendered identifies N+1; eager loading collapses the loop into a join or one batched lookup.
A larger pool runs the same 101 queries with more parallelism — neither the count nor the per-request round-trip cost changes.
A cache hides the pattern behind hit rate: cold pages and invalidation still storm the database, and correctness now depends on a second system.
`customers.id` is the primary key and already index-backed; each lookup is fast — the problem is that there are `n` of them.
variants.interviewTip: Quote the scaling law, not the snapshot: 'queries grow as 1 + n with page size' diagnoses N+1 in one sentence and shows you measured before reaching for infrastructure.
